Cervantes. Miguel de Cervantes was a Spanish writer and poet born in fifteen forty-seven whose masterwork Don Quixote stands as one of literature's greatest novels and a foundational work of the modern novel form. He lived during Spain's Golden Age, experiencing military service, captivity, poverty, and finally literary triumph late in life. His innovative narrative technique, psychological depth, and satirical exploration of chivalry and reality established him as a defining figure of Spanish cultural achievement.

Born in Alcalá de Henares in central Spain, Cervantes lived through Spain's imperial peak under Philip the Second and Philip the Third. In fifteen seventy-one, he participated in the Battle of Lepanto as a galley soldier and lost the use of his left hand to a gunshot wound—an experience that informed his later writing and military knowledge. He was captured by Barbary corsairs and held for ransom in Algiers from fifteen seventy-five to fifteen eighty. His family ransomed him, and these years of captivity and suffering shaped his later works.

He published La Galatea in fifteen eighty-five, a pastoral romance that gained moderate recognition. He worked in various administrative positions and experienced financial instability throughout his life. The breakthrough came with Don Quixote, published in two volumes in sixteen oh-five and sixteen fifteen. The novel became an immediate sensation across Europe, translated into English and French within years. It made Cervantes famous but not wealthy.

Don Quixote pioneered the modern novel through psychological realism, narrative complexity, embedded stories, and metafictional awareness of the novel as a form. These distinguished it from earlier prose narratives. The novel satirizes chivalric romance traditions while exploring themes of reality versus illusion, idealism versus pragmatism, and the power of storytelling and imagination. He continued writing plays, poetry, and shorter works, including the Novelas ejemplares in sixteen thirteen, until his death in sixteen sixteen—just one day before William Shakespeare. He is considered the greatest Spanish writer of all time. His story connects him to Spain as his birthplace and cultural context, to Don Quixote as his masterpiece and arguably the first modern novel, to Spanish literature where he is the canonical figure, to the Renaissance as a late Renaissance figure whose work synthesizes and transcends Renaissance literary conventions, to Spain's Golden Age when he lived during the nation's imperial and cultural peak, to Madrid where he spent his later years, to satire as exemplified by Don Quixote, and to chivalry as the primary target and theme of his masterwork.
